works.Federkopfschmuck des Moctezuma|Azteken,: The headdress is about 1.16 metres high and 1.75 metres wide. It is made of some 400 long, iridescent green tail feathers of the quetzal bird, together with turquoise cotinga, pink spoonbill and brown feathers, set with more than a thousand small gold plates. Whether Moctezuma II wore it himself is not documented; it probably reached Europe soon after the conquest of Mexico. In 1596 it is listed in the collection of Archduke Ferdinand II at Ambras Castle; today it is shown at the Weltmuseum Wien. After a joint Austrian–Mexican restoration it rests in a vibration-damped showcase. Mexico has asked for its return, but experts consider transport too dangerous for the brittle feathers.
works.Mona Lisa|Leonardo da Vinci, um 1503: The portrait very probably shows Lisa Gherardini, wife of the Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo. Leonardo began it around 1503 and kept working on it until the end of his life. With “sfumato” — soft transitions without hard outlines — the face and the smile seem alive and hard to pin down. In 1911 the painting was stolen from the Louvre and found in Florence only two years later; since then it has been the most famous painting in the world.
works.Mädchen mit dem Perlenohrring|Johannes V: The picture is not a portrait of a particular person but a “tronie” — a study of a head, an expression and a costume. The girl wears an exotic turban and an oversized pearl; the dark background makes the face and the light stand out. For the blue, Vermeer used precious ultramarine made from lapis lazuli. The small painting hangs in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.
works.Selbstbildnis|Rembrandt van Rijn, 1659: Rembrandt painted this self-portrait three years after his bankruptcy, at the age of 53. He shows himself without flattery: tired eyes, wrinkles, heavy ageing skin, built up from thick, vigorous layers of paint. The light falls only on the face; everything else sinks into darkness. The painting belongs to the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
works.Selbstbildnis|Vincent van Gogh, 1889: Van Gogh painted this self-portrait in September 1889 in the asylum at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, which he had entered of his own accord after his breakdowns. Background and suit are steeped in the same cool blue and shot through with swirling brushstrokes, from which his orange-red hair glows. It is one of his last self-portraits; today it hangs in the Musée d’Orsay in Paris.
works.Die Arnolfini-Hochzeit|Jan van Eyck, 143: The double portrait shows the merchant Giovanni Arnolfini from Lucca and his wife in their house in Bruges. Every detail — the little dog, the chandelier, the oranges, the wooden clogs — is painted in oil with the utmost precision. The convex mirror on the back wall reflects two more people, and above it is the inscription “Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434” — “Jan van Eyck was here”. Whether a wedding is really depicted is still debated today.
works.Bildnis Adele Bloch-Bauer I|Gustav Klimt: Adele Bloch-Bauer was the wife of a Viennese sugar industrialist and a patron of Klimt. Her face and hands are finely painted, while her dress and the background dissolve into ornaments of gold leaf. In 1938 the Nazis seized the painting; only in 2006, after a long legal battle, did the heir Maria Altmann get it back. Today it hangs in the Neue Galerie in New York.
works.Selbstbildnis im Pelzrock|Albrecht Dürer: Dürer shows himself at 28, strictly frontal, symmetrical and with long curly hair — a pose until then reserved for images of Christ. He understood the artist’s power to create as a divine gift. Every hair, and every hair of the fur, is painted individually. The painting hangs in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich.
works.Sternennacht|Vincent van Gogh, 1889: Van Gogh painted “The Starry Night” in June 1889 in the asylum at Saint-Rémy, from the view out of his window before sunrise — he added the village from memory. Swirls, eleven stars and a glowing moon move across the sky; in the foreground a dark cypress rises like a flame. He himself did not think the painting a success. Today it is one of the best-known paintings of all and hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
works.Der Wanderer über dem Nebelmeer|Caspar D: A man stands on a rock and looks out over a sea of fog from which peaks rise. We see him only from behind, as a “Rückenfigur” — so we look into the landscape with him. The painting combines the sublimity of nature with the question of man’s place in it and is regarded as the emblem of Romanticism. It belongs to the Hamburger Kunsthalle.
works.Die große Welle vor Kanagawa|Katsushika: The colour woodblock print comes from the series “Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji”. A huge wave with claw-like spray threatens to swallow three boats, while Fuji stands small and calm in the background. Hokusai used the new Prussian blue imported from Europe. Hundreds of impressions of the print exist; it is one of the best-known images in the world.
works.Die letzte Fahrt der Temeraire|William T: The “Temeraire” was a 98-gun warship that had fought at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805. In 1838 a small, dark steam tug towed her up the Thames to be broken up. Turner depicts the farewell to the age of sail against a blazing sunset. He called the painting “my darling” and never sold it; today it hangs in the National Gallery in London.
works.Der Kuss|Gustav Klimt, 1908: A pair of lovers kneels at the edge of a flower meadow, wrapped in a shared golden cloak. The man’s robe bears angular ornaments, the woman’s round and floral ones. The painting was made at the height of Klimt’s “Golden Period” and was bought by the Austrian state while still on show at its first exhibition in 1908. It hangs in the Upper Belvedere in Vienna.
works.Der Schrei|Edvard Munch, 1893: A figure with a skull-like face covers its ears on a bridge while the sky seems to surge in red and orange. Munch described an experience at sunset in Kristiania, today’s Oslo: he had felt “an infinite scream passing through nature”. There are several versions; this one of 1893, in tempera and crayon on cardboard, hangs in the National Museum in Oslo.
works.Blaues Pferd I|Franz Marc, 1911: A young blue horse stands before a colourful, hilly landscape. For Marc, colours had their own meaning: blue stood for the masculine, the austere and the spiritual. The painting was made in the year the “Blue Rider” was founded and shows his path from observing nature to symbolic colour. It belongs to the Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus in Munich.
works.Komposition VIII|Wassily Kandinsky, 1923: The painting was made during Kandinsky’s time at the Bauhaus in Weimar. Circles, triangles, lines and grids float freely on a light ground — clearly drawn instead of the stormy patches of colour of his earlier works. Kandinsky considered it a high point of his work after the First World War. It belongs to the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York.
works.Komposition II in Rot, Blau und Gelb|Pie: Black horizontal and vertical lines divide the white surface; a large red field dominates the picture, while a small blue and a yellow one keep it in balance. With this Mondrian sought a universal harmony beyond the visible world. The apparent simplicity is itself the result of long, precise deliberation. The painting belongs to the Kunsthaus Zürich.
works.Der Tanz|Henri Matisse, 1910: Five red figures dance in a circle on a green hill against a deep blue sky — the picture needs no more colours. The Russian collector Sergei Shchukin commissioned it, together with its companion piece “Music”, for the staircase of his Moscow mansion. The circle is open at one point, as if the dance were pressing on. Today the painting hangs in the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg.
works.Senecio|Paul Klee, 1922: A round head made of geometric fields in orange, yellow and red, with two unequal eyes. The title alludes to “senex”, Latin for old man, and to the plant groundsel; the picture is at once a mask, a face and a colour study. Klee painted it in oil on gauze during his time at the Bauhaus. It belongs to the Kunstmuseum Basel.
works.Dame mit dem Hermelin|Leonardo da Vinci,: The painting shows Cecilia Gallerani, the young mistress of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan. The ermine was a symbol of purity and at the same time an emblem of Ludovico; the animal’s Greek name, “galē”, alludes to her family name. The turn of head and body was unusually lively for portraits of the time. The painting hangs in the Czartoryski Museum in Kraków.
works.Das Abendmahl|Leonardo da Vinci, 1495–14: Leonardo painted the mural in the refectory of the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. It shows the moment after Jesus’ words “One of you will betray me” — the apostles react in groups of three with alarm and questions. Instead of true fresco, Leonardo painted on dry plaster, which is why the picture began to decay during his lifetime. A restoration from 1978 to 1999 uncovered what survives.
works.Johannes der Täufer|Leonardo da Vinci, 1: John steps out of the darkness, smiles mysteriously and points upwards — to Christ, whose coming he announces. The reed cross and the fur are barely visible. It is probably Leonardo’s last painting. He took it with him to France; today it hangs in the Louvre.
works.Die Erschaffung Adams|Michelangelo Buona: The fresco is part of the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican, which Michelangelo painted from 1508 to 1512. God, borne by angels, stretches out his hand towards Adam; between the fingers a narrow gap remains, across which life is about to leap. The two hands are among the most quoted images in the history of art.
works.Die Verkündigung|Leonardo da Vinci, um 1: The angel Gabriel kneels before Mary in a garden and announces the birth of Jesus. Leonardo painted the picture as a young man in the workshop of his teacher Andrea del Verrocchio in Florence; it is considered one of his earliest works. His interest in nature already shows: the angel’s wings are painted after birds’ wings, and the landscape dissolves into haze. The painting hangs in the Uffizi.
works.Tondo Doni|Michelangelo Buonarroti, um 1: The round painting shows the Holy Family and was probably made for the marriage of the Florentine merchant Agnolo Doni to Maddalena Strozzi. The figures are modelled as powerfully as sculptures and intertwined in a bold twisting movement; nude youths stand in the background. It is the only finished panel painting securely attributed to Michelangelo and still hangs in its original frame in the Uffizi.
works.Die Delphische Sibylle|Michelangelo Buon: In antiquity the Sibyl of Delphi was a seer; Christianity saw in her a pagan prophetess of the coming of Christ. Michelangelo painted her on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel with a scroll in her hand, her head turned aside in surprise. She is one of five sibyls enthroned there alongside seven prophets.
works.Das Jüngste Gericht|Michelangelo Buonarr: More than twenty years after the ceiling, Michelangelo painted the entire altar wall of the Sistine Chapel. Over 300 figures whirl around Christ as judge of the world: the blessed rise, the damned plunge into hell. The many nude bodies caused outrage; after Michelangelo’s death some of them were painted over. In the skin held by Saint Bartholomew one sees a self-portrait of the artist.
works.Felsgrottenmadonna|Leonardo da Vinci, 14: Mary kneels with the infant Jesus, the young John and an angel in front of a dark rocky grotto. Leonardo links the figures through glances and gestures into a pyramid and bathes them in soft light. There are two versions: this earlier one hangs in the Louvre, a later one in the National Gallery in London.
works.Vision nach der Predigt|Paul Gauguin, 18: Breton women in white caps have a vision after the Sunday sermon: Jacob wrestling with the angel, as the Bible tells it. A tree trunk divides the picture into the real and the dreamed world, both on a glowing red ground. With flat areas of colour and clear outlines, Gauguin broke here for good with Impressionism. The painting hangs in the Scottish National Gallery in Edinburgh.
works.Ia Orana Maria|Paul Gauguin, 1891: The title is Tahitian for “Hail Mary”. Gauguin transferred the Christian Annunciation to the South Seas: Mary and the infant Jesus are Tahitians with haloes, and an angel with yellow wings stands among blossoms. He took the pose of the two praying women from a relief at the Javanese temple of Borobudur. The painting belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.
works.Woher kommen wir? Wer sind wir? Wohin ge: Gauguin painted this picture, almost four metres wide, on Tahiti at a time of illness, poverty and despair; afterwards he attempted suicide. It is read from right to left: from the infant through middle life, where a figure picks a fruit, to the old woman awaiting death. Gauguin himself saw it as his artistic testament. It hangs in the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston.
works.Arearea|Paul Gauguin, 1892: The Tahitian title means “pleasure” or “amusement”. Two women sit in the foreground, one playing a flute; behind them figures dance before the statue of a god. The red dog, mocked at the time, shows Gauguin’s free handling of colour. The painting hangs in the Musée d’Orsay in Paris.
works.Der gelbe Christus|Paul Gauguin, 1889: Christ crucified in a Breton autumn landscape near Pont-Aven, surrounded by peasant women in traditional dress. The model was a painted wooden crucifix in the chapel of Trémalo. The strong yellow, the dark outlines and the flat fields of colour are typical of Gauguin’s “Synthetism”. The painting belongs to the Buffalo AKG Art Museum in the USA.
works.Selbstbildnis|Paul Gauguin, 1885: Gauguin painted himself at the easel in a cramped attic in Copenhagen, where he was living with the family of his Danish wife. He had just given up his job as a stockbroker, hardly sold a picture and felt a stranger there. The sidelong glance and the crowded narrowness reflect this crisis. It is his first important self-portrait.
works.Manaò tupapaú|Paul Gauguin, 1892: The title means roughly “The spirit of the dead keeps watch”. A young Tahitian woman lies on a bed, full of fear of the spirit of the dead sitting behind her. The model was Teha’amana, Gauguin’s native wife, then about 13 years old — a circumstance viewed critically today. The painting belongs to the Buffalo AKG Art Museum.
works.Zwei Tahitianerinnen|Paul Gauguin, 1899: Two women stand close together, one carrying mango blossoms in a bowl. The calm, almost monumental bodies against the flat green background recall sculptures. The painting was made during Gauguin’s second stay on Tahiti, when he was already ill and in debt. It belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.
works.Gefleckte Pferde|Grotte du Pech Merle, L: Two horses stand back to back, their bodies and surroundings covered with black dots, with negative hand prints all around — outlines of hands around which paint was sprayed. The painting is some 25,000 years old. For a long time the dots were taken for a symbol; genetic studies have shown that horses with leopard-spotted coats really existed at that time.
works.Saal der Stiere: Auerochsen und Pferde|H: The “Hall of the Bulls” is the first large chamber of Lascaux Cave. Huge aurochs, up to five metres long, move across the rock ceiling in black outlines, with horses and deer among them. The painters used the curves of the rock to give the animals bodies. This photo shows a faithful replica.
works.Saal der Stiere: Rote Kuh und Pferde|Höh: A red cow with a black head, below it a row of small dark horses. For red and yellow the painters used ochre, for black charcoal and manganese oxide; the paint was dabbed on, applied with brushes of hair or moss, or blown through tubes. The photo shows a faithful replica.
works.Pferdefries|Grotte Chauvet, Ardèche · um: Four horses’ heads, staggered one behind the other, below them aurochs and two rhinoceroses fighting with their horns. The outlines were drawn in charcoal and smudged with the fingers to create shadow and roundness. This assurance in perspective and movement surprised researchers, for the pictures are some 36,000 years old.
works.Löwenfries|Grotte Chauvet, Ardèche · um: In the deepest chamber of Chauvet Cave a pride of cave lions hunts a herd of bison. The lions’ heads overlap as if they were moving forward together — almost like the frames of a film. Cave lions had no mane; the painters knew the animals well. The photo shows a replica.
works.Das „Chinesische Pferd“|Höhle von Lascau: The yellow horse with a black mane in the “Axial Gallery” of Lascaux got its nickname because its light, sweeping execution reminded people of Chinese ink painting. Around the horse are arrow- or plant-like signs and a grid-like rectangle whose meaning is unknown. The photo shows a replica.
works.Saal der Stiere: Großer Auerochse|Höhle: The head of a great black aurochs, a wild ox that became extinct in 1627. Strong outlines, horns in slightly twisted perspective and the nostrils are captured in a few lines. Beside it run smaller red deer. The photo shows a faithful replica.
works.Bisons im Salon noir|Grotte de Niaux, Ar: In the “Salon noir”, deep inside the cave, the animals are drawn only in black lines. In a few sure strokes the bison show hump, beard and coat. Some animals are marked with arrows, which has been interpreted as hunting magic — no one knows for certain. The photo shows a replica.
works.Zwei Bisons|Grotte de Niaux, Ariège · um: Two bison face each other, head to head. The drawing is sparing: an outline, a few lines for coat and horns — and yet the mass and tension of the animals can be felt. The photo shows a replica from the Prehistoric Park at Tarascon-sur-Ariège.
works.Whistlers Mutter|James McNeill Whistler,: The actual title is “Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1”: Whistler saw the picture above all as a composition of colours. It shows his mother, Anna McNeill Whistler, in profile, seated stiffly and calmly on a chair. In the USA it became a symbol of motherhood and even appeared on a postage stamp. It hangs in the Musée d’Orsay in Paris.
works.Der Seerosenteich|Claude Monet, 1899: A Japanese wooden bridge spans Monet’s water-lily pond at Giverny, surrounded by dense greenery. He had laid out the garden himself and diverted a stream to feed the pond. In the following decades he painted the pond and its water lilies some 250 times, in the end so freely that water, sky and bank merged into fields of colour. This version hangs in the National Gallery in London.
works.Impression, Sonnenaufgang|Claude Monet,: Monet painted the harbour of Le Havre in the morning haze, with an orange-red sun and a few quick strokes. At the first group exhibition in 1874 the critic Louis Leroy mocked the title and called the whole group “Impressionists” — the name stuck. The painting hangs in the Musée Marmottan Monet in Paris.
works.Der Heuwagen|John Constable, 1821: An empty hay wain crosses a ford of the River Stour in Suffolk; on the left stands the cottage of the farmer Willy Lott, which still exists today. Constable painted the landscape of his childhood after numerous sketches made on the spot. Little noticed in England at first, the painting won a gold medal in Paris in 1824. It hangs in the National Gallery in London.
works.Mandelbrot-Spirale (Relief)|Fraktal nach: For every point c of the number plane, z → z² + c is computed again and again: if z stays bounded, c belongs to the Mandelbrot set; otherwise the speed of escape determines the colour. This picture is not loaded but computed live by the graphics card, with light and shadow like a relief. In the close-up you can zoom in about 10²³-fold — ever new spirals and small copies of the whole set appear.
works.Der Traum|Henri Rousseau, 1910: A naked woman lies on a red sofa in the middle of a dense jungle, among lions, birds, an elephant and a snake charmer playing a flute. Rousseau explained that the woman is dreaming she has been transported into the jungle. It is his last large painting, made in the year of his death, and hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
works.Maria|Vierfarb-Sprayschablone, 2026: The portrait takes shape here before the viewer’s eyes. It begins with the photo, then the spray painting follows from light to dark, plate by plate. First sun yellow lays in face and shoulders, coral pink sets the shadows, petrol blue fills background and depths, and finally deep black draws hair, eyes and brows. Each layer covers part of the one before; only the last makes the face legible. The image area measures 360 × 450 millimetres.
works.Pietà|Michelangelo Buonarroti, 1498–1499: Mary holds the dead Christ on her lap, young and calm, without the despair shown in earlier depictions. Michelangelo made the group at about 24 for the tomb of a French cardinal in Rome. So that the grown body would fit on her lap, he let Mary’s robe spread out in wide folds. It is the only work he signed: his name is on the band across her breast. The original stands in St Peter’s Basilica, behind glass since the hammer attack of 1972; what is scanned here is a plaster cast from Copenhagen.
works.Durchbohrter Würfel · auf einer Ecke ste: A stepped bore leads into each of the six faces, from 50 to 20 millimetres in diameter, plus a 10-millimetre passage along each axis. The bores are so deep that those of neighbouring faces cut into one another: what remains are four nested cube frames around a small core cube, joined by webs along the space diagonals. So everything remains a single solid. Here it stands on a corner with an edge length of 80 centimetres, the opposite corner exactly vertically above.
works.Vase „Evolution“ mit Sonnenblume · vierf: The vase is designed for 3D printing and is 20 centimetres high in the original; here it stands four times as large in brushed copper, with a sunflower in it. From bottom to top its cross-section changes from a triangle through square, pentagon and hexagon into a circle, turning by 90 degrees on the way — this development gives it its name. The lettering “Evolution” in Brush Script is raised and rises at an angle on a single pentagon face. The wall is 2.5 millimetres thick, the base 3 millimetres, and the opening measures 76 millimetres.
works.David|Michelangelo Buonarroti, 1501–1504: Michelangelo carved the David at 26 from a huge block of marble that other sculptors had already started on and abandoned. He shows the biblical hero not after the victory but before the fight with Goliath: tense, alert, the sling over his shoulder. With its base the figure is 5.17 metres high and became the symbol of the free Republic of Florence. Since 1873 it has stood in the Galleria dell’Accademia; a copy stands in front of the Palazzo Vecchio.
works.Goldmaske des Tutanchamun · dreifach ver: The mask lay directly on the face of the mummy and was meant to give the king an eternal, perfect face in the afterlife. It is made of about ten kilograms of gold, inlaid with lapis lazuli, quartz, obsidian and coloured glass; the original is 54 centimetres high. On the brow sit the vulture and the cobra, the protective goddesses of Upper and Lower Egypt. Howard Carter found it in the tomb in 1925; it is now in Cairo.
works.Osiris · in Gold|Casa Museu Eva Klabin,: Osiris was the ruler of the afterlife and the god of rebirth. According to the myth his brother Seth murdered him; his sister and consort Isis put the dismembered body back together and conceived by him their son Horus. He is shown as a mummy with green or black skin, wearing the atef crown — the white crown of Upper Egypt between two ostrich feathers — and holding crook and flail before his chest, the signs of kingship. Every dead king, and later every dead person, became “an Osiris” at the judgement of the dead. Believers donated statuettes like this one to his sanctuaries, above all in the Late Period and especially at Abydos. The original, about 29 centimetres high, belongs to the Egyptian collection of the Casa Museu Eva Klabin in Rio de Janeiro; the archaeologist Moacir Elias Santos reconstructed it as a 3D model from photographs.
works.Büste der Nofretete · dreifach vergrößer: Nefertiti was the chief wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten; her name means “the beautiful one has come”. The limestone bust with a painted layer of stucco probably served as a model in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose — which is why the inlay is missing from the left eye. A German excavation under Ludwig Borchardt found it at Amarna in 1912. It is in the Neues Museum in Berlin; Egypt demands its return.
works.Der Denker|Auguste Rodin, 1880–1904: The figure was created in 1880 for the Gates of Hell, a bronze portal after Dante’s Divine Comedy, and was at first called The Poet: Dante was to sit above the fall of the damned and conceive his work. Taken on its own, it became an image of thought itself, tensing the whole body down to the curled toes. In 1904 Rodin had it cast enlarged; today there are more than twenty casts of this size, one of them in Paris in front of the Musée Rodin, where the artist is buried.
works.Venus von Milo|Alexandros von Antiochia,: A farmer found the statue in 1820 on the Cycladic island of Melos in the remains of an ancient building; a French naval officer saw to it that it came to Paris. The figure of Parian marble, a good two metres high, probably represents Aphrodite, the goddess of love, whom the Romans called Venus. The arms were already missing when it was found, and their original position is still unknown. It has stood in the Louvre since 1821.
works.Venus von Willendorf · zwölffach vergröß: The little figure was found in 1908 during excavations at Willendorf in the Wachau, prompted by the building of the Wachau railway. It is only eleven centimetres high, carved from limestone, and bore traces of red ochre; its face is hidden under a hairstyle or head covering. At about 29,500 years old it is one of the oldest representations of a human being. Whether it embodies fertility, a goddess or an ideal of beauty is unknown. The original is in the Natural History Museum in Vienna.

artists.Casa Museu Eva Klabin: Eva Klabin (1903–1991) came from a family of industrialists and over decades collected art from five millennia: Egyptian, Greek and Roman antiquities, Chinese porcelain, European paintings and furniture. She left her house on the Rodrigo de Freitas lagoon in Rio de Janeiro, together with the collection, to a foundation; since 1995 it has been a museum that shows the rooms as she lived in them.
artists.Azteken: The Aztecs, who called themselves Mexica, founded their capital Tenochtitlan in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, where Mexico City stands today. From there in the 15th century they ruled an empire of tributary cities reaching from the Gulf coast to the Pacific. To them featherwork was more precious than gold; specialised craftsmen, the amanteca, made shields, garments and headdresses from it for rulers and images of gods. Moctezuma II reigned from 1502; in 1519 Hernán Cortés landed on the coast, and in 1521 Tenochtitlan fell.
artists.Auguste Rodin: Auguste Rodin (1840–1917) is regarded as the founder of modern sculpture. He was rejected three times by the Paris art academy and worked for a long time as a decorative plasterer before he became famous — and at the same time fiercely attacked — for his rough, animated surfaces. Much of his life was devoted to the never-completed Gates of Hell; The Kiss also grew out of this work.
artists.Alexandros von Antiochia: Almost nothing is known about the sculptor. His name was on a fragment of the base found together with the figure in 1820 and lost afterwards; it named Alexandros, son of Menides, of Antioch on the Maeander. He was one of the Greek artists of the Hellenistic period who drew on older models from the Classical age.
artists.Leonardo da Vinci: Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was a painter, sculptor, engineer and natural scientist of the Italian High Renaissance. He trained in Florence in Verrocchio’s workshop, worked for many years at the Sforza court in Milan and died in France in the service of King Francis I. Only about fifteen of his paintings survive, along with thousands of notebook pages on anatomy, optics, water and machines.
artists.Johannes Vermeer: Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675) lived and worked in Delft. He painted slowly and left only about 35 pictures, mostly quiet interiors with one or two figures in the light of a window. After his death he was almost forgotten; he was rediscovered only in the 19th century.
artists.Rembrandt van Rijn: Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn (1606–1669) was the most important painter of the Dutch Golden Age. In Amsterdam he became famous and wealthy with portraits and history paintings, but went bankrupt in 1656. No painter before him portrayed himself so often: some 80 self-portraits in oil, etching and drawing show him from a young man into old age.
artists.Vincent van Gogh: Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890) only began painting at 27 and in just ten years created some 860 paintings. In Paris he got to know the Impressionists; in the south of France he found his luminous colours and his forceful brushstroke. Hardly noticed in his lifetime, he is now regarded as one of the founders of modern painting.
artists.Jan van Eyck: Jan van Eyck (c. 1390–1441) was court painter to Duke Philip the Good of Burgundy and worked mainly in Bruges. He refined oil painting in thin, glazed layers to the point where fabrics, metal and light seem almost tangible. With the Ghent Altarpiece, made together with his brother Hubert, he created one of the major works of Early Netherlandish painting.
artists.Gustav Klimt: Gustav Klimt (1862–1918) was a co-founder and the first president of the Vienna Secession, which broke with academic art in 1897. His pictures combine ornament, symbolism and erotic motifs; in his “Golden Period” he used real gold leaf, inspired by the Byzantine mosaics of Ravenna. He is regarded as the most important painter of Viennese Art Nouveau.
artists.Albrecht Dürer: Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528) of Nuremberg was a painter, engraver and theorist. Two journeys to Italy acquainted him with Renaissance art, which he brought to Germany. His woodcuts and engravings spread throughout Europe and made him famous in his own lifetime.
artists.Caspar David Friedrich: Caspar David Friedrich (1774–1840) was the most important painter of German Romanticism. He lived in Dresden and painted landscapes as an expression of inner feeling: fog, moonlight, ruins and people seen from behind. Long forgotten after his death, he was rediscovered in the 20th century.
artists.Katsushika Hokusai: Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849) was a Japanese painter and woodblock artist of the Edo period. In his long life he used more than thirty artist’s names and created tens of thousands of pictures, prints and sketches, among them the “Manga” sketchbooks. His prints strongly influenced the European Impressionists in the 19th century.
artists.William Turner: Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775–1851) was an English painter who studied at the Royal Academy from the age of 14. He painted light, weather, steam and sea ever more freely, until forms dissolved into colour. He bequeathed his estate of almost 300 paintings and thousands of drawings to the British nation.
artists.Edvard Munch: Edvard Munch (1863–1944) was a Norwegian painter and printmaker. Illness and death in his family shaped his art, which depicts anxiety, love, jealousy and loneliness. With his “Frieze of Life” he became a forerunner of Expressionism.
artists.Franz Marc: Franz Marc (1880–1916) was a Munich painter who in 1911 founded the artists’ group “Der Blaue Reiter” (The Blue Rider) with Wassily Kandinsky. He painted mainly animals, in which he saw a purer, unspoilt nature, and gave colours their own meaning. He was killed in the First World War at Verdun in 1916.
artists.Wassily Kandinsky: Wassily Kandinsky (1866–1944) was born in Moscow and gave up a career in law to become a painter in Munich. He is regarded as one of the founders of abstract painting and compared colours and forms with the tones and sounds of music. From 1922 to 1933 he taught at the Bauhaus.
artists.Piet Mondrian: Piet Mondrian (1872–1944) was a Dutch painter who moved from naturalistic landscapes through Cubism to pure abstraction. With the De Stijl group he developed “Neoplasticism”: only horizontal and vertical lines, the three primary colours plus black, white and grey. His visual language has shaped architecture, design and fashion to this day.
artists.Henri Matisse: Henri Matisse (1869–1954) was the leading figure of the Fauves, the “wild beasts”, who around 1905 used colour freely and independently of nature. Alongside Picasso he is regarded as the most important artist of classical modernism. In old age, when he could hardly paint any more, he created coloured paper cut-outs with scissors.
artists.Paul Klee: Paul Klee (1879–1940) was born near Bern and was a painter, graphic artist and musician. He taught at the Bauhaus from 1921 to 1931 and created some 10,000 works, often small, poetic and full of humour. The Nazis denounced his art as “degenerate”; he returned to Switzerland in 1933.
artists.Michelangelo Buonarroti: Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564) was a sculptor, painter, architect and poet of the Italian Renaissance. He worked for the Medici in Florence and for several popes in Rome, where he painted the ceiling and the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel and designed the dome of St Peter’s. Even in his lifetime he was called “il Divino”, the divine one.
artists.Vierfarb-Sprayschablone: The technique comes from street art and the screen printing of Pop Art: a photo is reduced to a few tonal values, and each tonal value becomes a stencil of its own. Here a Python program calculates the separation, adds bridges so that no island falls out of the plate, and produces the cutting contours for four plates of 1-millimetre PETG measuring 420 × 510 millimetres.
artists.CAD-Entwurf: The cube is a parametric model, written in Python with the CAD library build123d. All dimensions depend on a few parameters in the program; the bore depths follow from a single value, the web thickness. The design measures 60 millimetres along each edge and is calculated to be manufactured as a closed, coherent solid.
artists.Parametrischer Entwurf: The shape is not modelled by hand but computed: a Python program defines five cross-sections with number of corners, size and twist and joins them over the height with cubic splines into a smooth surface. The corners are rounded by 6 millimetres so that they remain printable. The manifold3d library turns this into a closed solid and wraps the lettering around the wall. The result is an STL file for the printer, a preview model in copper and a technical drawing.
artists.Paul Gauguin: Paul Gauguin (1848–1903) was first a stockbroker and painted as a Sunday painter before turning to art full-time in 1883. In Brittany, with flat colours and dark outlines, he developed “Synthetism”; in 1891 he moved to Tahiti, later to the Marquesas Islands, where he died. His search for the “primitive” strongly influenced modernism — his image of the South Seas and his relations with very young native women are viewed critically today.
artists.Grotte du Pech Merle: The cave of Pech Merle near Cabrerets in the Lot département was discovered in 1922 by two teenagers. It contains paintings and engravings from several periods of the Palaeolithic, including negative hand prints, mammoths and footprints in clay. Unlike Lascaux and Chauvet, the original can still be visited today in small groups.
artists.Höhle von Lascaux: Lascaux Cave in the Vézère valley (Dordogne) was discovered in 1940 by four teenagers. Its roughly 600 paintings and 1,500 engravings are about 17,000 years old. Because visitors’ breath and lights made algae and mould grow, the original has been closed since 1963; faithful replicas such as Lascaux II and Lascaux IV can be visited.
artists.Grotte Chauvet: Chauvet Cave in the Ardèche was discovered in December 1994 by Jean-Marie Chauvet, Éliette Brunel and Christian Hillaire. Its pictures are some 36,000 years old, more than twice as old as those of Lascaux. The cave is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and closed to the public; since 2015 a replica, the “Grotte Chauvet 2”, has shown its pictures.
artists.Grotte de Niaux: The Grotte de Niaux lies in the Pyrenees in the Ariège département. Its “Salon noir”, deep inside the mountain, contains bison, horses, ibex and deer drawn in charcoal and manganese oxide, about 14,000 years old. Niaux is one of the few painted caves whose original can still be visited, by torchlight in small groups.
artists.James McNeill Whistler: James Abbott McNeill Whistler (1834–1903) was an American painter who lived mainly in Paris and London. He championed the idea of “l’art pour l’art” — art for art’s sake — and gave his pictures musical titles such as “Arrangement”, “Nocturne” or “Symphony”. His lawsuit against the critic John Ruskin also became famous.
artists.Claude Monet: Claude Monet (1840–1926) was at the centre of the Impressionists, who painted outdoors to capture changing light. He often painted the same motif in whole series at different times of day, such as haystacks or Rouen Cathedral. From 1883 he lived at Giverny, where his garden with the water-lily pond became the main subject of his late years.
artists.John Constable: John Constable (1776–1837) was an English landscape painter from Suffolk. Again and again he painted the countryside of his childhood along the River Stour and studied clouds and sky in numerous oil sketches made in the open air. In France, where he won a gold medal in 1824, he influenced the Barbizon painters and later the Impressionists.
artists.Fraktal nach Benoît Mandelbrot: Benoît Mandelbrot (1924–2010) was a French-American mathematician who did research for many years at IBM. In 1975 he coined the term “fractal” for shapes that resemble themselves at ever smaller scales, such as coastlines, clouds or ferns. The set named after him was first made visible with computers around 1980 and became a symbol of chaos theory.
artists.Henri Rousseau: Henri Rousseau (1844–1910) was a customs official in Paris — hence his nickname “le Douanier”, the customs officer — and taught himself to paint. His jungle pictures were based on visits to the botanical garden and the zoo; he never left France. Smiled at at first, he was revered by Picasso and the avant-garde and is regarded as the leading representative of naïve painting.
artists.Ägypten: Tutankhamun came to the throne around 1332 BC as a child of about nine and died around 1323 BC at about 19. Under him Egypt returned to the old gods after Akhenaten’s Amarna period. Politically he was an insignificant ruler; he became famous only through his almost untouched tomb in the Valley of the Kings, found by Howard Carter in 1922.
artists.Thutmosis: Thutmose was chief sculptor at the court of the pharaoh Akhenaten in the newly founded capital of Amarna. His name is known from an inscription on an ivory horse blinker found in his house. His workshop contained numerous portraits of the royal family, many of them unfinished — they show how the sculptors of the Amarna period worked.
artists.Gravettien: The Gravettian is an Upper Palaeolithic culture of about 33,000 to 22,000 years ago, named after the site of La Gravette in the Dordogne. People hunted mammoth, reindeer and horse and sometimes lived in large camps. From this period come numerous small female figures of stone, ivory and clay, found between France and Siberia.
